posts.body_html:
So apparently, one way to distinguish S. rosea from a purpurea venosa is by flower color: venosas have red flowers whereas roseas have pale, pinkish to white colors. Hmmm, not sure if that works anymore, there's red flowered populations in northern Baldwin Co, AL! This population is literally hundreds of miles away from the closest venosa population.

posts.body_html:
You've hit the nail on the head, with the pigment issue. In general, pigment is a poor criteria in taxonomy. Pigment genes too easily change within a species, sometimes even on one plant. Even leaf shape is often an unreliable taxonomic guide; oaks and maples can show great diversity within a species.

We've got "roseas" (actually purp. venosa burkii...heh heh!) from Baldwin, and they have a lot of variation on pitcher shape, flower color, etc. Some have hoods that fold like "montana", while others are wide open. When one compares these southern plants with, say mid Atlantic types, there seems to be greater range in morphology in the southern plants. Well, there used to be.

Pretty flower, whatever it is!

posts.body_html:
seriously....I've had this population for a very long time and didn't realize until now that there are some crazy BULBOUS clones in the mix! What the F man, this is crazy! suppose having them crammed in a community tray and neglected for more than a decade didn't help....these are divisions from my mother plants. For now, I'm calling this clone S. rosea 'bulbous' Northern Baldwin Co, AL, pics taken 9/9/21. This is a newly opened pitcher:


It really needs space to stretch out its feet and intense lighting to get the shape...or so I think? No clue how this phenotypic variance thing works, the traps on this clone can look normal and not very bulbous. Here's the first bulbous trap that was noticed, it colored up a bit now that it has aged:




Not sure whether to say "wha-DAYAM!" or "HOT-DAYAM!," hard to say what's more in vogue these days:
